title: Which websites and tools help with case interview prep?
description: An honest overview of free and paid case interview websites, partner-practice platforms, coaching and drills, and how to choose.
hook: There are many case prep websites, and it is easy to spend more time collecting resources than practising. Here is an honest map of the main options, free and paid, so you can choose a small set and get on with practising.
body:
Free first

  • The firms' own pages: the best place to start. Our list of official cases.
  • PrepForCase: a free course, over 100 cases with worked answers and interviewer scripts, and drills for maths, structuring, charts and sizing. No paywall.
  • University consulting clubs: many publish casebooks and run practice sessions.

Popular prep websites

  • PrepLounge: known for its community for finding practice partners, plus cases and coaching.
  • CaseCoach: video courses and cases from former consultants.
  • RocketBlocks: drills for case skills such as maths, charts and structuring.
  • Management Consulted, Hacking the Case Interview, IGotAnOffer, StrategyCase: large libraries of articles and firm guides, with paid courses and coaching.
  • Victor Cheng's CaseInterview.com: free videos and materials on his approach.

Coaching

One-to-one coaching from former consultants can be valuable a week or two before final rounds, to get expert feedback. It is expensive, so use it to fix specific weaknesses after plenty of free practice, not as a starting point.

How to choose

  1. Pick one main source for learning and one for cases.
  2. Find a practice partner, or two.
  3. Use drills for weak spots.
  4. Stop collecting; start practising.

Choose resources by the skill they help you improve

A large library of cases is useful only if you know what to practise. If your issue is structure, a short timed prompt with a model answer is more efficient than another full 40-minute case. If you lose accuracy under time pressure, practise mental arithmetic aloud and explain units. If you freeze during recommendations, record ten 45-second conclusions and review them for clarity and evidence.

Use a simple diagnostic after every mock: give yourself a score from one to five for understanding the objective, structure, analysis, synthesis and communication. Add a note describing the specific point at which the case became harder. Five cases with the same error should trigger a targeted drill rather than five more unstructured attempts.

Before buying coaching or a subscription, ask what feedback it provides, how much practice you will actually use and whether it supports the interview format you face. Free official firm resources and peer practice are often sufficient to build the fundamentals. Paid help is most valuable when it gives you expert, specific feedback you cannot obtain elsewhere, not access to another stack of generic frameworks.
